title: Policy reforms will be made for a global unicorn company in Nepal: Prime Minister - The Rising Nepal
description: Policy reforms will be made for a global unicorn company in Nepal: Prime Minister  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Kathmandu, Oct 31: Prime Minister Balendra Shah has said that promotion of game development and the information technology (IT) sector in Nepal could foster an environment conducive for Nepali businesses to prosper in the international market and evolve into global unicorns.

Taking to his social media account today, Prime Minister Shah has mentioned that all necessary regulations and conditions will be assessed for this purpose. He noted that there are companies that have gained international recognition by developing gaming applications in Nepal, highlighting that the globally renowned Ludo (approximately 200 million downloads) and Callbreak game (over 150 million downloads) were created by Nepali developers.

Furthermore, he mentioned that numerous young individuals are keen on developing gaming applications. "We reached out to them to understand their challenges and discussed ways to simplify the game development sector, advancing it as an industry. We have now commenced the groundwork to address their issues," Prime Minister Shah said.

The Prime Minister has in the social media post noted that IT-related 'products' and exports are currently in a very favorable condition, and considering our capabilities, the ease of earnings for companies, reinvestment opportunities, tax simplifications, and policy reforms and well as regulations concerning international income will be streamlined.

Additionally, the Prime Minister has mentioned that investments will be directed towards the overall ecosystem to benefit the IT product and gaming industry comprehensively through game jams, startup events, hackathons, through regular engagements with the information technology sector, and the Rastra Bank and the Ministry of Finance. title: Nepal detains journalists to warn rest of free press - Nepali Times
description: Nepal detains journalists to warn rest of free press  Nepali Times
publisher.title: Nepali Times
full_article:
Whenever Nepal's autocrats wanted to warn the media during the absolute monarchy days, they arrested a few journalists on a Friday.

That is what the state apparatus did on 30 October, leading to muted protests over the weekend. Plainclothes police officers entered newsrooms to nab reporters following a story about state highhandedness.

Photo: ANUP TAMU / FACEBOOK

In the past, authoritarian regimes wanted everyone to know they were behind the detention, but Prime Minister Balendra Shah's office denied any involvement, insinuating that Nepal Police chief Inspector General Dan Bahadur Karki was miffed about media coverage regarding efforts to sack him.

But then on Friday night, the Police said it had been acting on the advisers' orders. For journalists covering their colleagues' detention, this was an impossible to verify case of he-said-she-said.

Even so, it was yet another indication that relations between the governing party and the government are not well. Worse, it could even be a worrying rift between the government and the security apparatus.

All photos: BIKAR RAUNIYAR

Plainclothes police officers made rounds of several media outlets across Kathmandu to question and detain journalists on Friday in a move that was widely condemned by the mediasphere, civil society, political leadership, and press freedom watchdogs.

Security officials took DNA Khabar editor-in-chief Dhiraj Basnet, Motive News editor Shobhraj Baral, and Nepal Press reporter Bishwamani Subedi into custody on Friday afternoon.

Subedi was said to have been detained on the basis of a letter from the Cyber Bureau after Nepal Press published news claiming that the government was considering relieving Inspector General Karki from his duties. Nepal Press newsroom leadership were questioned about their sources.

Basnet was called in by the Kathmandu Valley Crime Investigation Office under the pretext of discussing an eSewa account number. Baral was similarly taken in without charges on vague grounds.

Officers also entered the Naya Patrika newsroom in an attempt to find journalist Nawaraj Mainali, who reported on the leaked WhatsApp coversation between a power broker and a Supreme Court justice.

Another police team went to Anamnagar to Diyo Post’s office looking for editor-in-chief Sudeep Bishwakarma and news coordinator Madan Dhungana, but left after failing to find them.

When pressed by journalists on the charge and documentation, police refused to provide them saying they were just acting on ‘orders from above’.

Naya Patrika broke the story earlier this week involving leaked correspondence between Supreme Court Justice Hari Phuyal and political fixer Imam Sapkota insinuating political interference in judicial proceedings. Other media outlets followed up on the piece, with coverage of corruption and collusion between judicial officials, political and security officials, as well as middlemen.

Detained journalists were released after a few hours, reinforcing the theory that this was to send a warning to the rest of the media not to step out of lione.

It is most likely that the PMO ordered the detentions despite denials by the prime minister's advisers. But it was condemned by figures across the political spectrum, most tellingly by leaders of the governing RSP itself. Spokesperson Jagdish Kharel, himself a former tv anchor, said the arrests violated press freedom and freedom of expression.

Many including in the press drew comparisons to the crackdowns on the press during Gyanendra’s rule after he staged a military-backed coup on 1 February 2005 when he sent the army into newsrooms to censor content, and detain pro-democracy journalists.

In a statement, the Federation of Nepalese Journalists called the detention of reporters by polics a blatant interference with press freedom’: ‘It is entirely inappropriate to resort to state terror if there are any grievances about news content instead of seeking resolution through established legal procedures. These actions violate the Constitution, domestic laws, and international legal standards.’

This is not the first time intimidation tactics against the press have been employed since the RSP government took office. In July, there was a coordinated blockade of the main gates of some media companies by illegally parked cars as a symbolic protest against the media coverage of the government's drives to curb traffic violations.

The RSP condemned the move then too, but social media accounts known to be associated with the Prime Minister's chief adviser supported the action. Nepal rans highest in South Asia for press freedom, however trolling and threats against journalists by the prime minister's supporters have led to a degree of self-censorship.

On Friday evening, Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s press adviser Deepa Dahal wrote on social media that the PM, his secretariat, and the PMO had no knowledge of the reporters’ detention, and that the PM had immediately instructed relevant authorities to release the detained journalists and refrain from newsroom crackdowns.

The reporters were released on Friday evening, and the Nepal Police also issued a clarification saying that the journalists were not detained, but brought in for 'routine questioning' on orders from the prime minister's office.

The denial of responsibility by the PMO and the security apparatus points to a disconnect, at least in public, between the two state institutions, at a time when the judicial arm of the state has also been dragged into the mud.

This seems to be an attempt at plausible deniability and finger pointing by the PMO and Police, and hints at a widening rift between Prime Minister Shah and The RSP Chair Rabi Lamichhane.

title: Nepal and Mauritius move closer to G2G labour agreement - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal and Mauritius move closer to G2G labour agreement  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Nepal and Mauritius have moved closer to signing a bilateral labour agreement that would allow Nepali workers to be recruited through a government-to-government (G2G) mechanism.

The High Commission of Mauritius in New Delhi formally conveyed its agreement to Nepal’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs on October 29, forwarding a revised draft of the proposed memorandum of understanding (MoU) to facilitate the recruitment of Nepali workers through the G2G system.

The proposed agreement aims to expand employment opportunities for Nepali workers in manufacturing, construction, agriculture, tourism and information technology, offering competitive salaries and benefits. It also seeks to promote safe and dignified foreign employment under the Employers Pay Principle, which requires employers, rather than workers, to bear recruitment costs.

The revised draft includes provisions for a government-led recruitment process, the selection of skilled and trained workers, and recruitment procedures in line with the laws of both countries. It also outlines employers’ responsibilities, workers’ rights and welfare provisions, and arrangements for repatriating workers after their employment contracts expire or are terminated.

The initiative follows a bilateral meeting between Nepal’s Minister for Youth, Labour and Employment Ramji Yadav and Mauritius’s Minister of Labour and Industrial Relations Mohamed Reza Cassam Uteem in Geneva, Switzerland, on June 9.

At the meeting, Yadav proposed expanding labour cooperation through a G2G mechanism. Uteem said that employers in Mauritius covered recruitment costs and expressed interest in creating more employment opportunities for Nepali workers.

He also proposed organising an international employment fair in Nepal to facilitate recruitment and strengthen labour cooperation between the two countries.

The Nepali government is now preparing to complete the necessary domestic procedures to finalise the revised draft MoU and move ahead with the proposed agreement.

The initiative is part of Nepal’s broader effort to strengthen labour diplomacy and diversify overseas employment destinations while reducing the costs and risks associated with foreign recruitment.

title: Sacred splendour at Siddhartha - Nepali Times
description: Sacred splendour at Siddhartha  Nepali Times
publisher.title: Nepali Times
full_article:
Worshippers gazing reverently at the face of a deity in a temple rarely wonder whose hands gave it shape. Unknown master artists of Kathmandu Valley passed on their skills within the family: a father, an uncle, a grandmother's brother, someone who learned the work at a family bench and inherited with it the duty of keeping it alive.

That chain of hands is the subject of the Siddhartha Art Gallery 39th anniversary exhibition brings together 36 traditional artists and artisans working in wood, stone, metal and paint.

Curated by museologist and artist Pradip Shakya, Sacred Splendor begins with a question rather than an answer: ‘What could be more profound than a life without suffering?’

He describes the Valley as a crucible where trade routes, pilgrimage paths and intellectual movements met, and where one of the world's most sophisticated artistic traditions took shape.

Deities throng the gallery space. The fierce protector Bhairav stands near the benevolent Ganesh. The serene Prajnaparamita, Avalokiteshvara and Vasundhara keep them company — they come from two faiths, yet they speak in one visual language of mudra and postures.

Shakya explains that tthe gestures of hand and body allows the viewer to understand the cause of suffering and the path to enlightenment. It is a language that has allowed Hinduism and Buddhism to flourish together in the Valley for over a thousand years.

The curator wanted to bring both traditions under one roof to show the tolerance of Nepali society. Sangita Shrestha of Dwarika's Hotel inaugurated the exhibition with Gautam Rana, founder of Baber Mahal Revisited.

"Our art is not in museums. It lives in the hands of the potter of Thimi, whose wheel has turned for a thousand years. It lives in the chisel of Patan, where stone still becomes god. It lives in the thangka and the mandala, where every line carries meaning. It lives in the lost-wax metal casting that travelled from Nepal to Tibet and beyond, and in the wood carving that gave Newar architecture its soul,” said Shrestha, whose own hotel is a haven for rescued artefacts.

"If we lose a building, we can rebuild it, but losing the artisans who know how to carve and continue the tradition would mean losing a thousand years of memory,” Shrestha added.

The life force of art, spirituality and tradition come together in this exhibition with the works by Pradip Shakya, Rabindra Shakya, Sundar Sinkhwal, Rajani Sinkhwal, Chandra Shyam Dangol, Palsangmo Lama, Jigme Tamang, Siddhi Ratna Shakya, Ujaya Bajracharya, Indra Prasad Silpakar and Ram Bhakta Maharjan, and the late Kalu Kumale.

Shakya notes that many of the works carry family skill and ancestral knowledge passed down through generations. A bronze figure cast today is made with the same respect for ancient texts as it was hundreds of years ago.

A gilded bronze, a paubha, a carved wooden beam: each comes from the same union of spiritual and artistic devotion. Here, a statue is not an object but a presence, one that is invoked, adorned and venerated. Shrestha's hope rests on the younger artisans in the show, who she said are carrying these skills to new heights.

Sangita Thapa of Siddhartha said the show brings a living tradition into view and presents the historic splendour of Nepali art in a single space. Devendra Thumkeli, former member secretary of the Nepal Academy of Fine Arts, said the exhibition shows how deeply art has shaped religious, cultural and social life in Nepal. Artist Prakash Mijar called it a landmark exhibition that joins spirituality, history and art, and urged that such original traditions be protected and encouraged.

The faces with serene half-closed eyes, wide eyed wrathful gazes, the hand gestures took someone a lifetime to learn. After 39 years of building a home for art, the Gallery has chosen to mark the occasion by honouring the hands that create the divinity in wood, metal. stone and in paintings. In the Shakya's own words, this is "a rare opportunity to witness the soul of a civilisation that continues to create beauty as a pathway to the divine”.

Sangeeta Thapa and the artist Shashikala Tiwari founded Siddhartha Art Gallery at Pratap Bhawan, Kantipath in 1987 to create a contemporary art space and meeting point for artists from Nepal and abroad.

Ten years later, the gallery moved to Baber Mahal Revisited, a complex where Gautam Rana had envisioned a gallery space, and the courtyard has been its home ever since.

More than 600 exhibitions later, the gallery has hosted artists from around the world and mounted retrospectives of all the big names in Nepal’s contemporary and traditional art. The Gallery also organised exhibitions of Nepali art in the UK, India, Pakistan,vBangladesh and at the Moesgaard Museum in Denmark.

The first Kathmandu International Art Festival in 2009 led to the founding of the Siddhartha Arts Foundation in 2011, and then the 2012 festival and the Kathmandu Triennale in 2017 and 2022. It co-commissioned the Nepal Pavilion at the Venice Biennale with Ang Tsherin Sherpa and took Nepali artists to the Kochi Biennale.

title: UN grants Nepal three more years to prepare for LDC graduation - myRepublica
description: UN grants Nepal three more years to prepare for LDC graduation  myRepublica
publisher.title: myRepublica
full_article:
KATHMANDU, Oct 31: The United Nations General Assembly has unanimously endorsed Nepal’s request for a three-year extension to prepare for graduation from the Least Developed Country (LDC) category.

(adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({});

Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lok Bahadur Paudel Chhetri informed the media that Nepal had secured an additional three years for its graduation preparations. The deadline for Nepal’s LDC graduation has now been extended to November 24, 2029, he said at a press conference held at the ministry on Friday.

Nepal had requested the extension, citing the impacts of national and international developments. The ministry had formally written to the United Nations seeking more time.

Nepal was originally scheduled to graduate from the LDC category in November 2026. The additional time will help the country prepare for a sustainable transition to developing-country status, Chhetri said.

Related story EU supports to build trade capacities of university professors...

At the press conference, the ministry also announced that the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) had decided to provide US$21.6 million in assistance to Nepal to support survivors of the Bhotekoshi floods of August 26.

Nepal had submitted a special request to the FRLD on August 31, seeking prompt assistance following the glacial disaster.

Chhetri also said that preparations were underway for Nepal’s high-level participation in the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31), scheduled to take place in Türkiye from November 9 to 20. During the conference, Nepal is preparing to sign a framework agreement on climate change cooperation with the Republic of Korea.

The ministry also informed that the 10th coordination meeting between the security forces of Nepal and India—the Armed Police Force and the Border Security Force, respectively—was held in Kathmandu. The meeting focused on strengthening border security and increasing surveillance to curb cross-border crimes.

On Thursday, Foreign Minister Sishir Khanal held a meeting with representatives of relevant ministries and agencies to assess the damage caused to the Rasuwagadhi border point, discuss the reconstruction of damaged infrastructure and explore the resumption of checkpoint operations.

The ministry is also holding consultations with concerned agencies to reopen other major border points with China.

According to the ministry, 860 Nepalis who had fallen victim to online and digital fraud were rescued from Southeast Asian countries, including Cambodia, Myanmar, Laos and Thailand.

A Nepali worker was killed in a drone attack in Saudi Arabia. Efforts are underway to repatriate his body, the spokesperson said.

The first ministerial meeting of BIMSTEC member states on home affairs was held in India, with Home Minister Sudhan Gurung attending. The meeting discussed ways to strengthen regional cooperation to combat cross-border crimes, human trafficking, cyberattacks and illicit financial flows.

The ministry also informed that 250,000 passports had been printed using the new system.
